Read together, they yield four sequenced stages, each pinned to a rising rung of the taxonomy and each equipped with a distinct AIGC entry point. The Learning stage handles knowledge input. The answer lies in how generative tools rearrange the flow of information reaching working memory. When an open-source text tool renders a script's structure visible, students no longer spend effort parsing formatting conventions or reconstructing narrative scaffolding by hand; that housekeeping is offloaded, and the presentation-driven demand that ordinarily clutters early learning thins out 37 . The revised Bloom taxonomy supplies an ordered ladder of cognitive objectives, while constructivist learning theory insists that knowledge is assembled by the learner rather than transmitted intact. Read together, they yield four sequenced stages, each pinned to a rising rung of the taxonomy and each equipped with a distinct AIGC entry point. The Learning stage handles knowledge input. Micro-lecture videos and interactive animations, generated with AIGC support, deliver foundational concepts in a form that keeps early extraneous demands low 38 . Comparable media designs in art and design programmes-augmented-reality frameworks for practice-based education 39 and animation-based problem-solving materials 40 -indicate that the delivery format itself carries part of the instructional burden. Instructor-student interaction here stays largely one-directional, and the output is judged by a recall-and-comprehension rubric. The Thinking stage lifts the target objective toward analysis: AI-driven problem scenarios prompt learners to interrogate what they have absorbed, forcing conceptual reconstruction rather than passive acceptance 1 . Assessment shifts to the quality of reasoning traces students leave behind. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 In the Applying stage, skill transfer takes over. Students turn to open-source animation software to realize concrete schemes, moving from understanding to execution 3 . The teacher's role becomes that of a troubleshooter, and deliverables are scored against technical fidelity and completion. The Creating stage sits at the apex of the ladder, where an AIGC co-creation platform hosts original animation projects 10 . Here human-machine collaboration is genuinely reciprocal, and originality, coherence, and expressive intent form the evaluation criteria. Figure 2 traces the full activity sequence and tool-embedding nodes across the four stages. The escalation across stages is deliberate rather than incidental. Learning targets recall and comprehension; Thinking moves to analysis; Applying demands transfer into production; and Creating asks for synthesis and original expression. Each stage also hands something forward, since the artefact and the competence produced at one stage become the entry condition for the next: a student who has already interrogated a script arrives at modelling with a plan rather than a blank scene. The four stages do not carry equal weight in assessment. Final work is judged against the Creating stage, while the earlier stages are assessed formatively, which keeps the evaluative emphasis on original output without leaving the preparatory work unmonitored 35 . analysis.discussion: Why did the AIGC-driven model pull extraneous load down while pushing germane load up? The answer lies in how generative tools rearrange the flow of information reaching working memory. When an open-source text tool renders a script's structure visible, students no longer spend effort parsing formatting conventions or reconstructing narrative scaffolding by hand; that housekeeping is offloaded, and the presentation-driven demand that ordinarily clutters early learning thins out 37 . The same logic extends to redundancy. Conventional animation instruction often forces learners to process the same content through several channels at once-verbal explanation layered over manual sketching-whereas the generative pipeline lets each channel do distinct work, trimming the duplicated processing that inflates extraneous load 13 . Freed capacity does not simply vanish, though. Fig. 9 Heatmap of standardized path coefficients linking the three cognitive load dimensions to the four creative thinking facets, with color intensity encoding effect magnitude and direction. Fig. 8 Scatter plot of creative thinking composite scores against intrinsic cognitive load, overlaid with the fitted quadratic curve. The vertex falls at a moderate load value, approximately 5.9 on the ninepoint scale, which is the pattern an inverted-U association implies. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 The generative activities in the Thinking and Creating stages demand that students evaluate, curate, and reassemble machine output, which is exactly the kind of effortful schema-building that germane load names 23 . The selective response of the facets asks for a different explanation. Fluency and flexibility trade largely on retrieval speed and category switching, capacities that improve with practice in either condition, so it is unsurprising that they rose in both groups without a group difference 28 . Originality and elaboration depend instead on deeper transformation-combining remote associates, refining a concept until it holds together-and these operations draw on precisely the schema-building resources that germane load names 30 . On this reading the intervention did not make students think more; it changed the quality of thinking that the freed capacity could sustain, which is why the advantage concentrated in the two facets most sensitive to deep processing. The correlations in Fig. 7 sharpen that account. Fluency and flexibility hang together closely, as they should if both index the breadth of an initial search through memory, and their joint insensitivity to condition suggests that the generative toolchain did not simply accelerate idea retrieval. Originality and elaboration form a separate and more moderate pairing, and their weak association with fluency matters for interpretation: had originality risen only because students produced more responses, its correlation with fluency should have been considerably higher than the 0.41 observed. The same two-part structure has emerged from factor analyses of the Torrance battery, where fluency-driven and transformation-driven components separate rather than collapse into a single dimension 31 . Set against the long-run decline in originality and elaboration documented for large samples, the present result reads as a modest counterpoint, since the facets hardest to move historically are the ones this intervention moved 46 . Ulger's finding that creative training can lift divergent-thinking scores without touching problem-solving is a useful caution in the other direction: facet-level gains need not generalise to the wider construct 29 . The inverted-U finding for intrinsic load carries a caution that the earlier sections could only foreshadow. Too little intrinsic challenge leaves creative reasoning underpowered, while too much saturates working memory and crowds out the generative operations creativity needs 34 . The practical lesson is that intrinsic load should be tuned rather than minimised. A teacher designing an AIGC-supported animation task ought to calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range-demanding enough to engage, restrained enough to leave room for exploration-rather than assuming that easier is always better 12 . This tempers a common but simplistic reading of load theory, and it is among the more transferable takeaways here. Set against prior work, these results are largely consonant but not identical. Studies pairing design thinking with germane load in STEAM settings likewise found creativity gains routed through deep engagement, which aligns with the mediation reported above 30 . The divergence lies in specificity: earlier flipped-learning and projectbased interventions reported broad creative-thinking improvement without partitioning which facets responded, so their apparent whole-scale gains may have masked the facet-level selectivity observed here 28 . Measurement grain is the likeliest reason for the discrepancy, since aggregating creativity into a single score can hide exactly the discriminant pattern that makes a mechanism legible 20 . Three implications follow for theory. The first concerns the status of germane load. Cognitive load theory has increasingly treated germane load as a redistribution of resources rather than an independent source of demand 14 , and the mediation estimate reported here gives that reconceptualisation an empirical foothold in a creative domain: germane load acted on originality and elaboration not directly but through a deep-processing strategy, which is what a redistribution account predicts. The second concerns the shape of the intrinsic-load effect. A curvilinear relation is hard to reconcile with the standard prescription to minimise load, and it suggests that the prescription was always domain-bound, holding for schema acquisition but not for tasks whose value lies in exploration. The third concerns creativity theory. Because the four facets responded differently to one instructional manipulation, treating divergent thinking as a single latent ability discards information that a facet-level model retains-an argument the creativity literature has long made on psychometric grounds 31 and that an intervention study can now make on experimental ones. For practice, the findings translate into three design rules rather than a general endorsement of generative tools. Assign generative assistance to the parts of a task that consume attention without building competence-formatting, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-77337-4 rendering, asset production-and keep it away from the parts where the struggle is the point. Make sure something recruits the freed capacity, because a lighter task is not automatically a more generative one; in the LTAC model the curation, evaluation, and reassembly demanded in the Thinking and Creating stages did that work. And calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range instead of smoothing it away. For animation programmes weighing curricular reform, an open-source toolchain can lower barriers to production while raising the ceiling on deep creative work, but only where the instructional design treats load as something to shape rather than merely shed 32 . That conditional is the substantive message for anyone hoping to scale generative tools across higher education in art and design 3 . This mixed-methods study, which leaned towards a qualitative design (qualitative dominant), investigated these issues among adult learners at a university in Ghana.
reading.findings: The results showed universal access to smartphones (99%), while 71% had access to a laptop. Adult learners in this cross-sectional survey reported a generally positive appraisal of their DWB. Overall, the DWB mean score (M = 4.58, SD = 0.76) is above the scale midpoint, indicating a favourable orientation towards GenAI use, although some variation exists across the well-being domains. The mental subscale showed modestly positive cognitive and psychosocial gains (M = 4.09, SD = 1.12), with the strongest item endorsements for improved problem-solving (M=4.94, SD=1.49), increased productivity (M=4.42, SD=1.59), greater decisiveness (M = 4.42, SD = 1.48) and feeling more cheerful (M = 4.42, SD = 1.64). The emotional subscale also reflected positive outcomes (M = 4.51, SD = 1.29), driven by items such as increased interest in new things (M = 5.08, SD = 1.46) and clearer thinking (M = 4.60, SD = 1.61). Following reverse coding, the physical DWB subscale recorded the highest mean (M = 5.14, SD = 1.45), with all indicators (sleep, eating, aches, and reduced exercise) scoring above the neutral point (4.93 ≤ M ≤ 5.37). However, item-level frequencies indicate that this pattern was not uniform. While most respondents selected the disagreement options, a minority reported physical strain: 17.0% reported disturbed sleep, 10.9% reported changes in eating habits, 16.5% reported physical discomfort, and 16.5% reported reduced physical exercise. Thus, although the overall trend suggests limited physical strain, less than half of the sample still experienced some bodily effects associated with GenAI use. For QoL, the composite mean (M = 2.06, SD = 0.94) shows that adult learners reported some improvement in daily functioning, safety, control, activity engagement, and time efficiency (Table 3). As accurately captured by Christodoulou and Zembylas23, technology acceptance is not a clear-cut matter of positive or negative attitudes but involves complicated stories and changes in relationships that affect the views and experiences of users. In the two phases of the study, adult learners' engagement with GenAI is characterised by coexisting gains and strain and not just a uniformly positive or negative experience. In the quantitative phase, DWB mean score was slightly above the 7-point Likert scale midpoint, with a meaningful minority of respondents reporting physical strain, and the composite mean of QoL indicated only modest gains in some aspects of GenAI-supported learning. The qualitative phase of the study throws further light on the mixed results in the survey; collaborators reflected on both appreciation for GenAI’s efficiency and anxiety over its encroachment on human creativity and authenticity. Using the unified ecological framework as a lens to understand the reciprocal and dynamic interrelationships between individuals, digital platforms, physical spaces, and macro-level factors, both findings highlight that adult learners’ DWB is a function of these interrelated factors. First, results from the survey and storytelling reveal that adult learners are knowledgeable of digital tools (including GenAI tools such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, etc.) and, on average, possess digital skills and competencies which they use to interact meaningfully across several digital platforms (i.e. Google, learning management systems). Second, interaction on digital platforms occurs at multiple levels and at different physical places (e.g. home, school setting) for some purposeful outcomes. Positive outcomes through GenAI use reflect gains (manifested as strengths) whilst the negative experiences Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:37204 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-78289-5 14 and outcomes create digital anxieties (afflictions). Third, GenAI use within the higher education context is constrained or limited by institutional-level factors (macro-level) such as policies on GenAI use, access to digital platforms and type of engagement. Thus, institutional factors mediate and shape adult learners' use of GenAI within this context. As such, adult learners' experiences of the extent to which their level of need and satisfaction is met through GenAI use reveal their state of well-being/wellness. Furthermore, both results highlight that within the higher education context, adult learners’ use of GenAI on a variety of digital platforms to perform academic and non-academic tasks is pervasive. Multiple digital connectivity at different places fosters a continuous cycle of constantly and actively creating and recreating their digital experiences, leading to cognitive and affective gains as well as embodied strains. Through such a process, they develop several coping systems which are mostly culturally embedded to counteract and adjust to the unpleasant physical afflictions. In sum, adult learners' digital well-being occurs through these nested multiple layers of influence (at the individual, meso and macro-levels), and is sustained by the powerful functionalities In addition, the results reveal that adult learners' positive gains with GenAI usage moderately influenced their cognitive, affective, and psychosocial well-being. For example, the qualitative arm of the study showed that adult learners appreciated the powerful functionalities of GenAI through enhanced efficiency in learning, but expressed psychological strain and apprehension. While it is true that GenAI tools like ChatGPT can enhance cognitive tasks, for instance, by making problem-solving activities easier, improving self-efficacy for task resolution and enhancing the quality and originality of solutions83, blind usage does not foster critical thinking and problem-solving, which are essential for academic and lifelong success15. Furthermore, the study found that some adult learners experienced minimal effects on their physical well-being as a result of GenAI usage, necessitating the development of self-adaptive coping mechanisms to alleviate the negative impacts of their digital experiences. Inferring from the unified ecological framework8, which illustrates a linkage between physical and digital domains influencing DWB when interacting with AI, the results imply that while GenAI usage may confer mental and emotional advantages, these are accompanied by modest but consistent reports of adverse bodily effects. Past studies have suggested that GenAI can reduce stress by streamlining tasks or creating a stress-free and emotionally supportive learning environment42,43,84, but excessive use of such technologies can lead to heightened anxiety, burnout, and sleep disturbance85.
